newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis talks shrouded in secrecy.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis talks shrouded in secrecy.

text.p: Moves to end Peru's 107-day-old hostage crisis were shrouded in secrecy on Thursday as government officials and peace brokers continued behind-the-scenes talks to reach a breakthrough.

Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, one of a team of three mediators, spent an hour on Thursday inside the Japanese ambassador's residence where about 20 heavily armed Marxist rebels have held 72 hostages in December 1996.

Vincent and fellow mediators, Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cirpiani and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, spent the last two weeks shuttling back and forth to the residence to kickstart negotiations stalled since March 12.
But there was little indication of progress and Cipriani acknowledged late on Wednesday that they had little to report.
"Information in these cases is limited due to the secrecy with which the issue is being handled," he said.

While mediators in Lima met with Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, leader of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels that burst in on the Dec. 17, 1996, cocktail party hosted by Japanese Ambassaor Morihisa Aoki, President Aberto Fujimori prepared to travel to Bolivia.
Fujimori, who has visited five foreign countries since the MRTA attack, was expected to discuss the crisis on Saturday with Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada.
Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio is among the hostages being held by MRTA, whose demands include the release of four MRTA militants held in Bolivian jails.

Fujimori, whose popularity rests largely on his tough line on terrorism, gave no sign of budging on the MRTA's main demand. Asked about the chance of a mass MRTA prisoner release, Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi said "there are some requests that are impossible to grant."
The hostages include Fujimori's brother, two ministers, military officers and Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
After three months of talks, mediators and hostages were showing signs of fatigue and frustration. Cipriani said this week that Peru's "heart is completely broken" by the siege.

Local daily La Republica reported on Thursday that Cerpa, convinced the crisis was headed for a violent ending, sent a farewell message to his wife, Nancy Gilvonio, serving a life sentence for involvement in MRTA activities in an Andean jail.
Gilvonio, married to Cerpa for 25 years and mother of his two children, is one of the roughly 400 MRTA comrades Cerpa wants freed in return for the release of the hostages.
